title: Demons do not belong to God
source_text: Ἐπεὶ δέ φησιν ἐν τούτοις ὁ Κέλσος ὅτι καὶ οἱ δαίμονές εἰσι τοῦ θεοῦ, καὶ διὰ τοῦτο πιστευτέον ἐστὶν αὐτοῖς καὶ καλλιερητέον κατὰ νόμους καὶ προσευκτέον, ἵν᾿ εὐμενεῖς ὦσι, διδακτέον καὶ περὶ τούτου τοὺς βουλομένους ὅτι ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος οὐδὲν τῶν φαύλων ἀναγορεύειν βούλεται κτῆμα θεοῦ τυγχάνειν, ἀνάξιον αὐτὸ κρίνων τηλικούτου κυρίου. διόπερ οὐ πάντες μὲν ἄνθρωποι χρηματίζουσιν ἄνθρωποι θεοῦ, μόνοι δὲ οἱ ἄξιοι τοῦ θεοῦ· ὁποῖος ἦν Μωϋσῆς καὶ Ἠλίας, καὶ εἴ τις, ἄλλος ἀναγέγραπται „ἄνθρωπος θεοῦ“ ἢ παραπλήσιός ἐστι τοῖς ἀναγεγραμμένοις. οὕτως δὲ καὶ οὐ πάντες ἄγγελοι „ἄγγελοι“ λέγονται εἶναι „τοῦ θεοῦ“ ἀλλὰ μόνοι οἱ μακάριοι, οἱ δ᾿ ἐκτραπέντες ἐπὶ τὴν κακίαν ἄγγελοι τοῦ διαβόλου ὀνομάζονται, ὥσπερ οἱ φαῦλοι ἄνθρωποι ἄνθρωποι ἁμαρτίας ἢ υἱοὶ λοιμοὶ ἢ υἱοὶ ἀδικίας. ἐπεὶ οὖν καὶ ἄνθρωποι οἱ μέν εἰσι σπουδαῖοι οἱ δὲ φαῦλοι, διὸ καὶ οἱ μὲν „τοῦ θεοῦ“ οἱ δὲ τοῦ διαβόλου εἶναι λέγονται, ἀλλὰ καὶ „ἄγγελοι“ οἱ μὲν „τοῦ θεοῦ“ οἱ δὲ τοῦ πονηροῦ, δαίμονες δὲ οὐκέτι διχῶς, πάντες γὰρ ἀποδείκνυνται εἶναι φαῦλοι· διὰ τοῦτο φήσομεν ψευδῆ εἶναι τὸν Κέλσου· λόγον εἰπόντος τό· εἰ δ᾿ εἰσί τινες δαίμονες. δηλονότι καὶ οὗτοι τοῦ θεοῦ· ἢ δεικνύτω ὁ βουλόμενος μὴ λόγον ὑγιῆ εἶναι τὴν περὶ ἀνθρώπων καὶ ἀγγέλων διαίρεσιν, ἢ λόγον ἔχοντα παραπλήσιον δύνασθαι ἀποδείκνυσθαι καὶ ἐπὶ δαιμόνων. Εἰ δὲ τοῦτ᾿ ἀμήχανον, δῆλον ὅτι οὔτε τοῦ θεοῦ εἰσιν οἱ δαίμονες· οὐ γὰρ ἄρχων αὐτῶν ὁ θεὸς ἀλλ᾿, ὥς φασιν οἱ θεῖοι λόγοι, ὁ „Βεελζεβούλ“·
pass_a_gloss: Since Celsus says in these that the demons too are of God, and therefore one must trust them and sacrifice with good omens according to laws and pray, that they be well-disposed, it must be taught (διδακτέον) about this too to the willing that the Word (λόγος) of God wishes to proclaim (ἀναγορεύειν) nothing of the base (φαῦλα) to be God's possession (κτῆμα θεοῦ), judging (κρίνων) it unworthy (ἀνάξιον) of so great a Lord. Therefore not all men are styled (χρηματίζουσιν) men of God (ἄνθρωποι θεοῦ), but only the worthy of God; such as Moses and Elijah, and if anyone else is recorded (ἀναγέγραπται) 'man of God' or is similar to those recorded. So also not all angels (ἄγγελοι) are said to be 'angels of God' but only the blessed (μακάριοι), while those turned aside (ἐκτραπέντες) to wickedness (κακία) are named angels of the devil (διάβολος), as base men are men of sin (ἁμαρτία) or sons of pestilence (υἱοὶ λοιμοί) or sons of injustice (υἱοὶ ἀδικίας). Since then men are some earnest (σπουδαῖοι) and some base, therefore some are said to be 'of God', some of the devil, and 'angels' some 'of God', some of the evil one (ὁ πονηρός), but demons no longer twofold (διχῶς), for all are shown to be base; therefore we shall say Celsus's statement false, saying: 'but if there are certain demons, clearly these too are of God'; or let him who wishes show either that the division (διαίρεσις) about men and angels is not a sound (ὑγιής) account, or that a similar account can be demonstrated also in demons. If this is impossible (ἀμήχανον), clear that neither are the demons of God; for their ruler (ἄρχων) is not God but, as the divine words (θεῖοι λόγοι) say, 'Beelzebul'.
pass_b_english: Since Celsus says in these words that the demons too belong to God, and that for this reason we must trust them, and offer acceptable sacrifices to them according to the laws, and pray to them, so that they may be well disposed, we must teach those who are willing about this point too: the word of God is unwilling to call anything wicked God’s possession, since it judges such a thing unworthy of so great a Lord. That is why not all men are called men of God, but only those who are worthy of God, such as Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1) and Elijah (1 Kings 17:24), and anyone else who is recorded as “a man of God,” or who is like those so recorded.

So too not all angels are said to be “angels of God,” but only the blessed ones; while those who turned aside to wickedness are named angels of the devil (Matthew 25:41), just as wicked men are called men of sin (2 Thessalonians 2:3), or sons of pestilence (1 Samuel 2:12), or sons of unrighteousness. Among men, then, some are good and some are wicked, and for this reason some are said to be “of God” and others of the devil (1 John 3:10); and among “angels” too, some are “of God” and others of the evil one. But demons are not divided in two in this way, for all of them are shown to be wicked.

For this reason we will say that Celsus’s argument is false when he says: “But if there are certain demons, clearly these too belong to God.” Or else let anyone who wishes show either that the division made concerning men and angels is not sound, or that an account like it can be demonstrated in the case of demons as well. But if this cannot be done, it is plain that the demons do not belong to God; for their ruler is not God, but, as the divine words say, “Beelzebul” (Matthew 12:24).

choices.choice: ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος here is taken as Scripture (‘the word of God’, lowercase), because the proof that follows is about how Scripture names men and angels (χρηματίζουσιν, ἀναγέγραπται, and ‘the divine words’ at the end of the chapter); a reading as the divine Word is possible but less likely. οὐδὲν ... ἀναγορεύειν βούλεται is rendered ‘is unwilling to call’, keeping βούλεται. Moses is called ‘man of God’ at Deuteronomy 33:1 (also Joshua 14:6, Psalm 90 title); Elijah at 1 Kings 17:24 (LXX 3 Kingdoms 17:24; also 17:18 and 2 Kings 1:9–13). ‘Sons of pestilence’ (υἱοὶ λοιμοί) matches LXX 1 Samuel 2:12 (1 Kingdoms 2:12), of Eli’s sons. ‘Sons of unrighteousness’ (υἱοὶ ἀδικίας) is left uncited: the nearest LXX phrase is the singular υἱὸς ἀδικίας (2 Samuel 7:10; 1 Chronicles 17:9), so the reference is not certain. ‘Of God ... of the devil’ cited to 1 John 3:10 (compare John 8:44, 47). ‘Angels of God’ is a general biblical phrase (e.g. Genesis 28:12, Luke 12:8) and is not tied to one verse. ‘Beelzebul’ as ruler of demons: Matthew 12:24 (also Mark 3:22, Luke 11:15). The sentence beginning δῆλον ὅτι οὔτε τοῦ θεοῦ εἰσιν οἱ δαίμονες is a ‘neither ... nor’ construction that runs on into chapter 26 (οὔτε πιστευτέον δαίμοσι); chapter 26 opens with ‘Nor’, so each chapter reads on its own without an added word. The leading ἢ of δεικνύτω is taken as ‘or else’.

'the Word of God will not declare ... since He judges it' to 'the word of God is unwilling to call ... since it judges such a thing' (βούλεται kept as unwillingness; ὁ τοῦ θεοῦ λόγος read as Scripture, since the proof is how Scripture names men and angels; note added)
